newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: New mix of drugs to help cancer victims - study.
newsitem.headline: New mix of drugs to help cancer victims - study.

text.p: New drug combinations could improve prospects for patients with advanced cancer of the breast, head and neck and bowels, studies presented at a cancer conference on Monday showed.
The reports were presented by drug company Rhone-Poulenc Rorer (RPR) at a four-day congress by the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) in Vienna.
In a phase I study on 42 patients, the firm combined new anti-cancer agent Taxotere and doxorubicin -- the most effective single agent currently used to treat breast cancer.
The patients, all of whom had an advanced stage of the disease, recorded an 88 percent response rate, demonstrating an improvement in their symptoms or a decrease in tumour size, RPR said.
Taxotere is approved in 35 countries to treat the disease in first-line therapy, treatment that follows once initial surgery combined with local chemotherapy has failed.

"This study is significant because it has showed us that the combination of Taxotere and doxorubicin is a highly active treatment for metastatic breast cancer," said Veronique Dieras of the Paris Curie Institute.
One in 10 women in Europe are known to develop breast cancer.
Joanna Horobin, Vice-President of the firm's oncology department, said it was too early to know if the combination treatment would boost survival chances of the disease.

"As we push these response rates to over 80 percent, that certainly would give a promise of some improvement in survival but that is too early to say," she told Reuters. "What we now need is to put this combination into large clinical studies."
Doxorubicin on its own can lead to heart failure, but the combination showed no major side effects and also attacked the cancer legions in other areas such as the liver, she said.
A phase II study conducted by RPR on 43 patients of head and neck cancer, particularly prevalent in the Far East, showed a response rate of 55 percent to a new combination of taxotere and cisplatin.
Previous rates were around 20 percent because of the aggressive nature of the disease and the fact that it is normally detected in a late stage.
"Having a good tested combination you can give to patients safely is probably going to open the door for physicians to try the combination in other tumours," she said.

Another phase II study involved 107 patients of colorectal cancer, which affects the large intestine or rectum. The second most common cancer worldwide, it has a 50 percent recurrence rate and a 20 percent response rate.

RPR is marketing a drug called Campto, which it says is the most effective drug currently available for treating the cancer at an advanced stage. Horobin said it would be introduced in most European markets in the first quarter of 1997.

"The message with Campto is that we've now got a treatment that will actually improve the symptoms. The patients will die anyway but this enables them to have six or eight more months of useful life," she said.
